title: Introduction to Astronomy
overview: A guided tour of the universe as astronomers understand it today, from the Earth-Moon system and naked-eye skywatching to planets, stars, galaxies and the Big Bang. It builds the vocabulary, scale intuition and observing habits that every other astronomy subject assumes. Because it uses everyday language and backyard observations, it is the standard entry point for curious beginners.

title: Mathematics and Physics Foundations
overview: The calculus, algebra and classical physics toolkit on which all quantitative astronomy rests: mechanics, gravitation, electromagnetism, waves and probability. Astronomy at the intermediate level and above is applied physics, so a firm grip on these subjects is the single biggest predictor of success. This pathway consolidates them with an astronomical flavor where possible.

overview: How stars form from interstellar clouds, shine by nuclear fusion, age, and die as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes. It progresses from observational properties to quantitative stellar structure.

title: Black Holes
overview: Black holes — stellar remnants and supermassive anchors of galaxies — are the most extreme objects in physics, where gravity dominates everything. The subject covers their formation, the relativity needed to understand them, observational evidence from X-ray binaries to the Event Horizon Telescope, and their role in galaxy evolution. It demands solid physics preparation and rewards it with the deepest insights in astrophysics.

title: Dark Matter and Dark Energy
overview: Roughly 95 percent of the universe is made of substances we cannot see directly: dark matter holding galaxies together and dark energy driving accelerating expansion. This subject examines the observational evidence — rotation curves, clusters, gravitational lensing, supernovae, the CMB — and the leading candidate explanations. It is the clearest signal that physics is incomplete.
